queued.critic_reason: New family on an untested universe (us-treasury-daily, 0 tests) with a coherent risk-premium mechanism (inflation-risk term premium compressing as yields revert). The rule is fully causal (rolling 252-day percentile, 50-day SMA exit), H.15 yields are point-in-time and public, and Treasury CFDs exist. At the claimed net Sharpe of 1.2 over 10 fresh years, t is about 3.8 against a bar of 3.0, and two instruments traded as one book double the data; costs on liquid bond CFDs are small. Whether the edge survives is for the statistics.
queued.data_source: US Treasury daily yield data (Federal Reserve H.15) and corresponding CFD price data
queued.mechanism: Investors demand a premium for holding nominal bonds during periods of high macroeconomic uncertainty or inflation volatility. When inflation expectations spike, the required term premium increases, causing nominal bond yields to rise and bond prices to fall. Patient capital willing to bear inflation risk buys these bonds at rich yields, capturing the premium as expectations stabilize and yields revert. This persists because inflation risk is systematic and cannot be diversified away by most investors, who face constraints on holding long-duration assets during high inflation.
queued.rule: At the daily close, compute the 10-year Treasury yield. If the current yield is in the top 10% of the rolling 252-day window, enter a long position in the 10-year Treasury CFD. Hold the position until the yield falls below its 50-day simple moving average, at which point exit to cash. If the yield is not in the top 10% at the close, remain in cash. This rule spans 2 instruments (the 10-year and 30-year Treasury CFDs) traded as one book.
queued.title: Treasury Inflation Expectations Risk Premium
queued.why: at its claimed strength it expects t 3.795 against 3.0 (passes 79% of the time); the claim must be verified at its source before it is built
queued.why_new: This is the first proposal in the risk premium class on the completely untested us-treasury-daily universe. While the general bond risk premium is well-documented in academic literature, it has not been tested as a daily CFD trading rule in a swap-free account, and the specific mechanism of inflation risk premium compression captured via yield-percentile mean reversion is new to this lab's registry.

today.data_source: Daily commodity futures index data (Bloomberg Commodity Index) and EM FX daily spot/CFD prices
today.mechanism: Many emerging market currencies are heavily commodity-exporter dependent. Commodity prices (measured by the Bloomberg Commodity Index) lead the respective EM FX currencies because commodity markets are more liquid and react faster to global macroeconomic news. The information diffuses from the commodity futures market to the thinner EM FX market with a lag of a few days. Global institutional investors trade the commodity futures first, while local exporters and central banks in EM countries hedge slowly, creating a persistent lag that can be captured by buying the EM FX after a strong commodity price move.
today.rule: At the daily close, if the Bloomberg Commodity Index has returned more than 1.5% over the past 3 days, and the corresponding commodity-linked EM FX currency (e.g., BRL, ZAR, COP, MXN) has returned less than 0.5% over the same 3-day window, enter a long position in that EM FX CFD. Hold the position for 5 trading days or exit immediately if the EM FX catches up and returns more than 1.0% from entry, whichever comes first. If no such currency meets the condition, stay in cash. This rule spans 4 commodity-linked EM FX currencies (BRL, ZAR, COP, MXN) traded as one book.
today.title: Commodity Price Lead-Lag in Emerging Market FX Currencies
today.why: At its own claimed strength the test cannot clear the bar: a net Sharpe of 1.0 over 8 fresh years gives t of about 2.8 against a bar of 3.000 before any costs, and the conditional 3-day trigger (BCOM +1.5% with the EM FX lagging) makes the effective bet count far smaller than daily. On top of that, EM FX CFDs (BRL, ZAR, COP, MXN) carry wide spreads against a 1.0% catch-up target, so the net claim is more than the evidence (none) could support.
today.why_new: This is the first proposal in the cross-asset linkage class on the completely untested em-fx-daily universe. While the commodity currency link is well-known in academic economics, the specific lead-lag trading rule exploiting the 3-to-5 day lag of EM FX relative to broad commodity index moves has never been tested in a swap-free CFD account, and it avoids the carry constraint by using short-term price momentum rather than interest rate differentials.

today.critic_reason: New family on an untested universe (us-etf-broad-daily, 0 tests) with a genuine information-diffusion mechanism (Hong-Stein style leader-laggard drift). The rule is causal (5-day ranks, fixed hold, no look-ahead), sector ETF daily history is public, and long-only ETF holding fits the swap-free account with negligible costs. At the claimed net Sharpe of 1.1 over 9 fresh years, t is about 3.3 against a bar of 3.0, and 10 ETFs traded as one book add breadth; whether the diffusion edge is real after the market's own drift is for the statistics.
today.data_source: Daily adjusted close prices of US sector and industry ETFs (from Yahoo Finance or Bloomberg)
today.mechanism: Information about economic conditions or sector-specific trends does not diffuse instantaneously across all sectors. Leading sectors (e.g., technology, financials, or energy) react first to macroeconomic news or earnings surprises, and lagging sectors (e.g., consumer staples, utilities, or REITs) react with a delay of several days. Institutional investors with large portfolios trade leading sectors first due to lower transaction costs or mandate constraints, while retail investors and smaller funds trade lagging sectors later, creating a persistent information diffusion drift that can be captured by buying the lagging sectors after the leaders have moved.

today.rule: At the daily close, rank a basket of 10 broad sector and industry ETFs (e.g., XLK, XLF, XLE, XLV, XLP, XLY, XLI, XLB, XLRE, XLU) by their 5-day returns. If the top-performing ETF (the leader) has returned more than 3.0% over the past 5 days, and the bottom-performing ETF (the laggard) has returned less than 0.5% over the same 5 days, enter a long position in the laggard ETF. Hold the position for 10 trading days or exit immediately if the laggard ETF catches up and returns more than 2.0% from entry, whichever comes first. If no such pair exists, stay in cash. This rule spans 10 sector and industry ETFs traded as one book.

today.why_new: This is the first proposal in the information diffusion class on the completely untested us-etf-broad-daily universe. While cross-industry information diffusion is a well-known academic phenomenon (Hong and Stein 1997), the specific sector rotation lead-lag trading rule exploiting the 5-to-10 day lag of laggard sector ETFs relative to leader sector ETFs has never been tested in this lab's registry, and it fits the swap-free condition perfectly because it requires only long positions in highly liquid ETFs with negligible overnight financing.
